title: Thrust Equation and Ideal Expansion
prompt: Write the rocket thrust equation and explain each term. For a fixed chamber and throat, why is thrust highest when the nozzle is perfectly expanded (P_e = P_a)?
answer: F = ṁV_e + (P_e − P_a)A_e. Maximum at P_e = P_a.
solution: From conservation of momentum: ṁV_e is momentum thrust and (P_e − P_a)A_e is pressure thrust. Underexpanded (P_e > P_a): extending the nozzle would turn that excess pressure into velocity more efficiently than it pushes on the exit plane, so you leave thrust on the table. Overexpanded (P_e < P_a): the extra bell area has pressure below ambient pushing against you, and severe cases cause flow separation. dF/dA_e = 0 exactly at P_e = P_a.

title: Isp, c* and Cf Explained
prompt: Define Isp, c* and Cf and how they relate. How does each change when you change propellants, and when you go from sea level to vacuum?
solution: Isp = F/(ṁg₀) = V_e/g₀ = c*·Cf/g₀, in seconds: how long 1 kg of propellant can produce thrust equal to its own weight. c* = P_c·A_t/ṁ is "combustion efficiency": the chamber pressure a given flow makes through a given throat. It depends only on propellant thermochemistry, roughly √(T_c/M) and γ. Cf = F/(P_c·A_t) is "nozzle efficiency": how much the nozzle multiplies the throat pressure force. It depends on expansion ratio, γ and ambient pressure. Changing propellant changes c*: LOX/CH₄ is about 330 s at sea level, LOX/H₂ about 450 s in vacuum thanks to low molecular weight, but H₂'s low density means big tanks. Changing atmosphere only changes Cf: Cf_vac = Cf_amb + P_a·A_e/(P_c·A_t). Real Cf is about 0.98 of ideal.
keyPoints: Isp = F/(ṁg₀) = c*·Cf/g₀
c* = P_c·A_t/ṁ, set by propellant (T_c, M, γ)
Cf = F/(P_c·A_t), set by nozzle and ambient pressure
Propellant change mainly moves c*; altitude only moves Cf
Isp vs density tradeoff (LOX/H₂ vs LOX/CH₄)

title: Vacuum Thrust Coefficient
prompt: An engine has a sea-level thrust coefficient Cf = 1.60. Chamber pressure is 10 MPa and the expansion ratio A_e/A_t = 20. Taking P_a = 101,325 Pa, what is its vacuum thrust coefficient?
solution:
Cf_vac = Cf_amb + P_a·A_e/(P_c·A_t) = 1.60 + 101,325 × 20 / 10×10⁶ = 1.60 + 0.203 ≈ 1.80.
The ambient term is back-pressure on the exit area, which disappears in vacuum. Isp rises by the same 13%.

title: Maximum Exhaust Velocity
prompt: Combustion products have chamber temperature 3500 K, mean molecular weight 22 kg/kmol and γ = 1.2. What is the theoretical maximum exhaust velocity (infinite expansion to vacuum, P_e = 0), in m/s? Why can a real nozzle never reach it?
solution:
V_e,max = √[(2γ/(γ−1)) · (R_u/M) · T_c] = √[12 × (8314/22) × 3500] ≈ 3984 m/s.
Reaching it would take an infinite expansion ratio and an isentropic nozzle. Real nozzles are finite and lose to friction, divergence, heat transfer and incomplete recombination.

title: Combustion Products and Isp
prompt: How do the properties of the combustion products relate to thrust and Isp? Why do LOX/H₂ engines run fuel-rich instead of at stoichiometric?
solution: V_e ∝ √(T_c/M), so Isp rises with flame temperature and falls with product molecular weight, and lower γ helps a little. Products set c*, and therefore Isp. LOX/H₂ runs at a mixture ratio of about 5–6 instead of stoichiometric 8 because the excess H₂ sharply lowers the mean molecular weight. That gains more than the small drop in T_c costs, and it also eases wall and turbine temperatures. Thrust itself is ṁV_e, so at fixed Isp you get thrust by moving more mass.
keyPoints: V_e ∝ √(T_c/M); γ is secondary
Product properties set c*
Fuel-rich H₂: lower M beats lower T_c
Cooler running is a side benefit
Thrust = ṁV_e: flow rate sets thrust, Isp sets efficiency

title: Graphite vs Copper Throat
prompt: Why would you use a graphite nozzle throat insert in one engine and a copper throat in another?
solution: Copper melts at 1085 °C but conducts heat extremely well (about 400 W/m·K), so it only works when actively cooled: a regen liner (GRCop, C-18150) moves throat heat flux into the coolant and runs indefinitely. A solid copper heat-sink chamber only survives seconds. Graphite (or carbon-carbon) survives uncooled at around 3000 °C, gets stronger with temperature, is light and handles thermal shock. It's used in solid motors and uncooled or ablative engines. Its weakness is oxidation and erosion by H₂O, CO₂ and oxidizer-rich gas, so A_t grows during the burn, which changes P_c and performance.
keyPoints: Copper: very high k, low melting point, so it must be regen-cooled
Copper heat-sink chambers are for short tests only
Graphite: uncooled, very high temperature, strengthens when hot
Graphite erodes or oxidizes, so the throat area grows
Choice follows cooling approach and burn duration

title: Why Nozzles Diverge
prompt: Why does a diverging section accelerate supersonic flow but decelerate subsonic flow? Derive the area-velocity relation.
solution: Continuity ṁ = ρAV gives dρ/ρ + dA/A + dV/V = 0. Momentum: dP = −ρV·dV. Speed of sound: dP = a²·dρ. Combining gives dρ/ρ = −M²·dV/V, so dA/A = (M² − 1)·dV/V. Subsonic (M < 1): density barely changes, so to speed up the area must shrink, like water in a hose. Supersonic (M > 1): density drops faster than velocity rises, so the area must grow to pass the same mass flow. Hence converging to M = 1 at the throat, then diverging.
keyPoints: Continuity in log-differential form
Momentum dP = −ρVdV and dP = a²dρ
dA/A = (M² − 1)dV/V
M < 1: velocity dominates; M > 1: density drop dominates
Choked throat at M = 1
Unlike: intimate mixing, high c* efficiency, fewer elements
Unlike: alignment and momentum-ratio sensitive, face heating, hypergol blow-apart
Like: tolerant, stable, flame off the face
Like: weaker mixing unless fans interleave
Pick by priority: performance vs robustness and stability
title: Like-on-Like vs Unlike Doublets
prompt: Why would you choose like-on-like doublets over unlike (fuel-on-oxidizer) doublets in an impinging injector, or the reverse? Give pros and cons of both.
solution: Unlike doublets impinge fuel directly on oxidizer, so mixing is intimate and c* efficiency is high with few elements. But they're sensitive to orifice alignment and momentum ratio (mixture-ratio maldistribution), they react close to the face (face heating), they're more prone to high-frequency instability, and hypergols can "blow apart" at the impingement point. Like-on-like doublets impinge fuel on fuel and ox on ox, making two fans that mix downstream. That's more tolerant of misalignment and momentum mismatch, keeps the flame off the face, and is generally more stable. The cost is less complete mixing (lower c* efficiency) unless the fans interleave well, and usually more elements.

keyPoints: GG dumps turbine flow at low Isp
More P_c means more dumped flow: a ceiling
FFSC: all flow ends up in the main chamber
Big turbine flow: power at low temperature, so high P_c
High P_c: more expansion, smaller engine, gas-gas mixing
title: FFSC vs Gas Generator Performance
prompt: Full-flow staged combustion is far more complex than a gas generator cycle. Why can it actually deliver more performance?
solution: In a gas generator cycle, the turbine drive gas (a few percent of total flow) is burned fuel-rich at a low, turbine-safe temperature and dumped overboard at low velocity. Every kilogram of it contributes almost no Isp. Raising P_c needs more turbine power, which means more dumped flow, so GG engines hit a P_c ceiling. In FFSC all the propellant goes through the preburners and turbines and then into the main chamber, so nothing is dumped. The huge turbine flow gives lots of power at modest temperature, which allows much higher P_c. That buys a higher expansion ratio for the same exit size, better sea-level Isp, a smaller and lighter engine, and gas-gas injection with high c* efficiency.

keyPoints: Turbine power limited to regen heat pickup
Required power scales with flow; heated area grows slower
Caps thrust and chamber pressure
Needs H₂/CH₄; RP-1 cokes
Fixes: more heated area, bleed expander
Pros: benign turbine temperature, restartable, reliable
title: Expander Cycle Limits
prompt: Explain the limitations of the expander cycle, including the square-cube argument for why expanders top out at modest thrust.
solution: In an expander, the only turbine energy is heat the fuel picks up in the regen jacket. Pump power scales with propellant flow (and P_c), and flow scales with throat area. Heated wall area grows more slowly, because for a fixed L* the chamber gets relatively shorter as it scales up. Heat available therefore falls behind the power required: square-cube in spirit. That caps thrust (RL10 and Vinci are on the order of 100–200 kN) and P_c. The fuel also has to absorb lots of heat and stay a clean gas, so hydrogen is ideal, methane works, and RP-1 doesn't (it cokes). The workarounds are longer or ribbed chambers, nozzle heat pickup, or a bleed (open) expander that dumps turbine flow at an Isp cost. Upsides: cool turbine gas, very reliable, easy restart.
